In July 2003, 80 plaintiffs from Russia, Ukraine, the Netherlands, and Kazakhstan turned to the European Court for
Human Rights, claiming that their right to life had been violated by Russian authorities' handling of the standoff. In April
2007, Igor Trunov, the claimants' advocate, reported that the ECHR had finally begun hearings into a complaint filed in
2003 by the victims against the Russian government. Trunov added that not only Russian citizens, but also those from
Ukraine, the Netherlands, and Kazakhstan, filed complaints in the <color=#3366CC>Strasbourg</color> Court. The plaintiffs demand €50,000
each in compensation for the violation of their human rights. The case was accepted by the court in December 2007.
On 8 July 2008, The Moscow Times reported that the hearings at the European Court of Human Rights would be
closed to the public at the request of Russian authorities as, according to Igor Trunov, they had "promised full
disclosure on how they handled the crisis", including "the makeup of the knockout gas used in the storming of the
theater by commandos."
On 20 December 2011, the European Court of Human Rights published its judgement in the case, ordering Russia to
pay the 64 applicants a total of 1.3 million euros in compensation. The court also found that Russia had violated Article
2 of the <color=#3366CC>European Convention on Human Rights</color> when handling the hostage crisis, "with inadequate planning and
conduct of the rescue operation", and with the "authorities' failure to conduct an effective investigation into the rescue
operation", although the Court found that there had been "no violation of Article 2 of the Convention on account of the
decision by the authorities to resolve the hostage crisis by force and to use the gas."
Chemical agent mystery and subsequent identification
It was reported that efforts to treat victims were complicated because the Russian government refused to inform
doctors what type of gas had been used. In the records of the official investigation, the agent is referred to as a
"gaseous substance". In other cases, it is referred to as an "unidentified chemical substance".
The Russian Federation, as a member-state of the Chemical Weapons Convention, undertook "never and under no
circumstances to carry out any activities prohibited to member-states of this Convention to develop, to accumulate, to
stockpile and to use chemical weapons that can cause death, temporary incapacitation, or permanent harm to humans
or animals." The Convention obliges the states to fulfill the conditions of toxic chemicals' use that allow to exclude or
considerably reduce the degree of injury and gravity of consequences. (The Convention allows the use of some
chemical agents like <color=#3366CC>tear gas</color> for "law enforcement including domestic <color=#3366CC>riot control</color>", but requires that "riot control agents"
have effects that "disappear within a short time following termination of exposure.")
Analysis of drug residue from the clothing of two British hostages and the urine of a third British hostage, by a team of
researchers at the British chemical and biological defense laboratories at Porton Down, <color=#3366CC>Wiltshire</color>, <color=#3366CC>England</color>, indicated
that two fentanyl derivatives had been used. Neither of those two were <color=#3366CC>fentanyl</color> or 3-methylfentanyl (the Russian
Minister of Health earlier said that fentanyl or one of its derivatives had been used, but did not specify which
derivatives).
The Porton Down analysis by James R. Riches and his colleagues showed that while fentanyl or 3-methylfentanyl were
absent from the urine of one survivor and residues of the agent in the clothing of two other British survivors, the
veterinary large animal sedative drug carfentanil and anesthetic agent remifentanil were identified by liquid
chromatographic tandem mass spectrometry in one hostage's urine and on the clothing of three hostages who had
returned to Britain after the hostage rescue. The authors concluded that carfentanil and remifentanil were used as a
mixture in the chemical agent employed by Russian troops to subdue the Chechen terrorists and hostages at the
Barricade Theater, perhaps suspended in the anesthetic agent <color=#3366CC>halothane</color>.
International reaction
• <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> – In unanimously adopting Resolution 1440 (2002), the <color=#3366CC>United Nations Security Council</color> condemned
the attack and demanded the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. The council also expressed
their sympathies and condolences to the victims, Russian people, and government of Russia, and urged all states
to cooperate with Russian authorities in bringing those responsible to justice.
• Ba'athist Iraq – Iraqi President <color=#3366CC>Saddam Hussein</color> condemned the attack in a television broadcast, arguing it would
ultimately benefit the United States and <color=#3366CC>Israel</color> in undermining <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>: "It's not wise for the Chechens to lose the
sympathy of Russia and the Russian people. The <color=#3366CC>tyrant</color> of our era is <color=#3366CC>Zionism</color> and America, and not Russia, <color=#3366CC>China</color>
or <color=#3366CC>India</color>."
In popular culture
In 2003, HBO broadcast Terror in Moscow, a documentary directed by Dan Reed. Interviews with hostages and
footage taken inside and outside the theater during the crisis are shown.
In 2004 a documentary by the BBC's Horizon investigated the gas that was pumped into the theater.
A Russian DLC released in 2005 for Postal 2 known as " " (Corkscrew Rules) contains a reference to the attack, in a
mission where the protagonist must defend himself from terrorists and police during an attack in a theater.
The 2006 play In Your Hands is based on the events of the Moscow theater siege, written by Natalia Pelevine, opened
in London at the New End Theatre. In April 2008, Pelevine said that Russian authorities had banned the play following
its Russian debut in the city of <color=#3366CC>Makhachkala</color>, the capital of <color=#3366CC>Dagestan</color> near Chechnya.
The play We Declare You a Terrorist, by Tim J. Lord and based upon the attack, premiered at the 2009 Summer Play
Festival.
The 2015 first-person shooter game Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege cites the crisis and FSB response as an
inspiration for their hostage rescue game mode.
Part III Episode 6 of the <color=#3366CC>Netflix</color> Spanish drama series <color=#3366CC>Money Heist</color> (La Casa de Papel) contains spoken references to
the theater crisis and the use of halothane gas, with critique of Putin's indifference to the fates of the hostages and
hostage-takers. In the series, Spanish authorities eventually use halothane gas to assault a bank during a hostage
crisis.
In Season 1 Episode 9 of, Bulgarian authorities nearly use poison gas to resolve a terrorist hostage-taking in a theater
in <color=#3366CC>Sofia</color>, which the <color=#3366CC>Federal Bureau of Investigation</color>, sent to assist Bulgarian authorities, strongly objects to. The standoff
is ultimately resolved without the gas being deployed.
The 2020 film Conference follows theater crisis survivor Natasha (Natalya Pavlenko) who returns to the theater to hold
a memorial, finally able to confront her survivor's guilt and her estranged daughter and husband. The film is by Russian
writer and director Igor I. Tverdovskiy.
Christopher Nolan's movie Tenet, released in August 2020, opens with a prologue that fans and critics have speculated
is based on the attack.
Western culture
Western culture, also known as Western civilization, European civilization, Occidental culture, Western society or
simply the West, is the externally cohesive yet internally diverse <color=#3366CC>culture</color> and <color=#3366CC>cultural heritage</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Western world</color>. The

term "Western" encompasses the <color=#3366CC>social norms</color>, <color=#3366CC>ethical values</color>, <color=#3366CC>traditional customs</color>, <color=#3366CC>belief systems</color>, <color=#3366CC>political systems</color>,
artifacts and <color=#3366CC>technologies</color> primarily rooted in <color=#3366CC>European</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> histories. A broad concept, "Western
culture" does not relate to a region with fixed members or geographical confines. It generally refers to the classical era
cultures of <color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color>, <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>, and their Christian successors that expanded across the Mediterranean
basin and <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and later circulated around the world predominantly through <color=#3366CC>colonization</color> and <color=#3366CC>globalization</color>.
The exact English phrase “Western civilization” appears to have become common in the late 1800s. One study notes
that it was being used without special explanation by at least 1890, while earlier 19th century English-language writers
generally talked about “European civilization”. Previous to that, "Christendom" was the only widely used umbrella
concept for centuries. Historically, scholars have closely associated the idea of Western culture with the <color=#3366CC>classical era</color> of
Greco-Roman antiquity. However, scholars also acknowledge that other cultures, like <color=#3366CC>ancient Egypt</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Phoenician</color>
<color=#3366CC>city-states</color>, and several <color=#3366CC>Near-Eastern cultures</color> stimulated and influenced it. The <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color> also promoted
<color=#3366CC>syncretism</color>, blending Greek, Roman, and Near-Eastern cultures. Major advances in literature, engineering, and science
shaped the Hellenistic Jewish culture, from which the earliest Christians and the Greek <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color> emerged. The
eventual Christianization of Europe in <color=#3366CC>late antiquity</color> would ensure that <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, particularly the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>,
remained a dominant force in Western culture for many centuries to follow.
The <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color>, after the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color>, were characterized by depopulation,
deurbanization, and the collapse of long-distance trade, as Europe suffered hundreds of years of raids and invasions
from Vikings, <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Magyars</color> from the north, south and east. Following that long period of war and instability,
however, medieval Europe experienced gradual improvements, including several <color=#3366CC>medieval renaissances</color>. <color=#3366CC>12th-century</color>
<color=#3366CC>Latin translations</color> brought ancient Greek and Roman texts back to central and western Europe from the Islamic world
and helped <color=#3366CC>medieval scholasticism</color> to grow and thrive. Medieval Christianity is credited with creating the modern
<color=#3366CC>university</color>, the modern hospital system, scientific economics, and <color=#3366CC>natural law</color> (which would later influence the creation

of <color=#3366CC>international law</color>). During the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, the rise of humanism, the spread of the <color=#3366CC>movable type</color> <color=#3366CC>printing press</color>, the
encounter with the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color> and the advance of the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color> each transformed European culture.
The <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color> of the 17th and 18th centuries advanced ideals of <color=#3366CC>empirical inquiry</color>,
political pluralism and <color=#3366CC>individual rights</color>. These ideas influenced <color=#3366CC>revolutions</color> across Europe and the Americas, spurred
the development of modern democratic institutions and, together with the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, transformed Western
society. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the influence of Enlightenment <color=#3366CC>rationalism</color> continued with the rise of <color=#3366CC>secularism</color>
and <color=#3366CC>liberal democracy</color>, while the Industrial Revolution fueled economic and technological growth. The expansion of <color=#3366CC>civil</color>
<color=#3366CC>rights</color> and the <color=#3366CC>decline of religious authority</color> marked significant cultural shifts. Tendencies that have come to define
modern Western societies include the concept of political pluralism, <color=#3366CC>individualism</color>, prominent <color=#3366CC>subcultures</color> or
<color=#3366CC>countercultures</color>, and increasing cultural <color=#3366CC>syncretism</color> resulting from <color=#3366CC>globalization</color> and immigration.
Terminology
The West as a geographical area is unclear and undefined. There is some disagreement about which nations should or
should not be included in the category, when, and why. Certainly related conceptual terminology has changed over
time in scope, meaning, and use. The term "western" draws on an affiliation with, or a perception of, a shared
<color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>worldview</color>, political, and religious heritage grounded in the Greco-Roman world, the legacy of the Roman
Empire, and medieval concepts of <color=#3366CC>Christendom</color>. For example, whether the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> or countries
influenced by its legacy, should be counted as "Western" is an example of the term's ambiguity. This can be traced to
the affiliation between the culture of ancient Rome and that of <color=#3366CC>Classical Greece</color>, a persistent Greek East and Latin
West language-split within the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>, and the permanent split of the Roman Empire in 395 into <color=#3366CC>Western</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> halves.
Some <color=#3366CC>philosophers</color> have questioned whether Western culture can be considered a historically sound, unified body of
thought. For example, <color=#3366CC>Kwame Anthony Appiah</color> pointed out in 2016 that many fundamental influences on Western
culture – such as <color=#3366CC>Greek philosophy</color> – are shared by the <color=#3366CC>Islamic world</color>. Appiah argues that the origin of the Western and
European <color=#3366CC>identity</color> can be traced to the 8th-century Muslim invasion of Europe via <color=#3366CC>Iberia</color>, causing Christians to form a
common Christian or European identity. Contemporary Latin chronicles from Spain referred to the victors in the
<color=#3366CC>Frankish</color> victory over the <color=#3366CC>Umayyads</color> at the 732 <color=#3366CC>Battle of Tours</color> as "Europeans" according to Appiah, denoting a shared
sense of identity.
Pope Leo III's transfer of the Roman Empire from the Eastern Roman Empire to the <color=#3366CC>Frankish</color> King <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> in the
form of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> in 800, the <color=#3366CC>Great Schism</color> of 1054, and the devastating <color=#3366CC>Fourth Crusade</color> of 1204 also
influenced what is considered the West.
As Europeans discovered the extra-European world, old concepts adapted. The area that had formerly been
considered the <color=#3366CC>Orient</color> ("the East") became the <color=#3366CC>Near East</color> as European countries began to interact with <color=#3366CC>Meiji Japan</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Qing China</color> in the 19th century. Thus the <color=#3366CC>Sino-Japanese War</color> in 1894–1895 occurred in the "<color=#3366CC>Far East</color>" while troubles
surrounding the decline of the Ottoman Empire occurred simultaneously in the Near East. The term "Middle East" in the
mid-19th century included the territory east of the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> but west of China—<color=#3366CC>Greater Persia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Greater</color>
<color=#3366CC>India</color>—but is now used synonymously with "Near East" in most languages. Stereotypical views of "the West" have been
labeled "Occidentalism", paralleling "<color=#3366CC>Orientalism</color>"—the term for the 19th-century stereotypes of "the East".
<color=#3366CC>Globalization</color> has spread Western ideas so widely that almost all modern cultures are, to some extent, influenced by
aspects of Western culture.
History
The earliest <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color> which influenced the development of Western culture were those of <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>; the area of
the Tigris–Euphrates river system. The area largely corresponds to modern-day <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>, northeastern <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>, southeastern

<color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> and southwestern <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, known as the <color=#3366CC>cradle of civilization</color>. <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egypt</color> similarly had a strong influence on
Western culture.
<color=#3366CC>Phoenician</color> mercantilism and the introduction of the alphabetical script boosted state formation in the Aegean and
current-day Italy and Spain, spawning civilizations in the Mediterranean such as <color=#3366CC>ancient Carthage</color>, <color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Etruria</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>.
The Greeks contrasted themselves with both their Eastern neighbors (such as the <color=#3366CC>Trojans</color>) as well as their Northern
neighbors (who they considered <color=#3366CC>barbarians</color>). Concepts of what is the West arose from the legacies of the <color=#3366CC>Western</color> and
the Eastern Roman Empire. Later, ideas of the West were formed by the concepts of Latin Christendom and the <color=#3366CC>Holy</color>
<color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>. Modern Western thought originates primarily from Greco-Roman and Christian traditions, with influence

from the <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> peoples, and includes the ideals of the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>.
The West of the Mediterranean Region during Antiquity
While the concept of a "West" did not exist until the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color>, the roots of the concept can be traced back to

<color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color>. Since <color=#3366CC>Homeric</color> literature (the <color=#3366CC>Trojan Wars</color>), through the accounts of the <color=#3366CC>Persian Wars</color> of Greeks

against <color=#3366CC>Persians</color> by <color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color>, and right up until the time of <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color>, there was a <color=#3366CC>paradigm</color> of a contrast
between Greeks and other civilizations. Greeks felt they were the most civilized and saw themselves (in the formulation
of <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>) as something between the advanced civilizations of the <color=#3366CC>Near East</color> (who they viewed as soft and slavish)
and the wild <color=#3366CC>barbarians</color> of most of Europe to the north. During this period writers like Herodotus and <color=#3366CC>Xenophon</color> would
highlight the importance of freedom in the Ancient Greek world, as opposed to the perceived slavery of the so-called
barbaric world.
<color=#3366CC>Alexander's conquests</color> led to the emergence of a <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic civilization</color>, representing a synthesis of Greek and
<color=#3366CC>Near-Eastern</color> cultures in the Eastern Mediterranean region. The Near-Eastern civilizations of <color=#3366CC>ancient Egypt</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, which came under Greek rule, became part of the Hellenistic world. The most important Hellenistic centre of

learning was <color=#3366CC>Ptolemaic Egypt</color>, which attracted Greek, Egyptian, Jewish, <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Phoenician</color> and even <color=#3366CC>Indian</color> scholars.
Hellenistic science, philosophy, <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, <color=#3366CC>literature</color> and art later provided a foundation embraced and built upon by
the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> as it swept up Europe and the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean world</color>, including the Hellenistic world, in its conquests
in the 1st century BCE in which the whole Mediterranean became essentially a Roman inland sea. The influence of
Hellenism coexisted in the Empire with a cultural divide between a predominantly Latin-speaking West and
Greek-speaking East. For about five hundred years, the Latin-speaking Western Roman Empire consisted of Western
Europe and Northwest Africa, while the Greek-speaking Eastern Roman Empire consisted of the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>. The "Greek" East was generally wealthier and more advanced than the "Latin" West. With the
exception of Italia, the wealthiest provinces of the Roman Empire were in the East, particularly Roman Egypt which was
the wealthiest Roman province outside of Italia.
From the time of Alexander the Great (the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color>), Greek civilization came in contact with Jewish civilization.
Christianity would eventually emerge from the <color=#3366CC>syncretism</color> of <color=#3366CC>Hellenic culture</color>, Roman culture, and Second Temple
Judaism, gradually spreading across the Roman Empire and eclipsing its antecedents and influences.Greek and
Roman <color=#3366CC>paganism</color> was gradually replaced by Christianity, first with its legalization with the Edict of Milan and then the
Edict of Thessalonica which made it the State church of the Roman Empire. <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color> Christianity, served as a unifying
force in Christian parts of Europe, and replaced or competed with some secular authorities. The Jewish Christian
tradition it had emerged from was all but extinguished, and <color=#3366CC>antisemitism</color> became entrenched in Christendom.
The birth of the European West during the Early Middle Ages
After the <color=#3366CC>fall of Rome</color>, much of Greco-Roman art, literature, science and technology was all but lost in the western part
of the old empire. Europe fell into a period of warring kingdoms and principalities now known as the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color>
(500–1000), marked by a continuation, or even intensification, of the destructive trends of <color=#3366CC>late antiquity</color>: depopulation,
deurbanization, and <color=#3366CC>barbarian</color> invasions. From the 7th until the 11th centuries, <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>, Vikings and <color=#3366CC>Magyars</color> raided
and invaded the <color=#3366CC>European peninsula</color> from the south, north, and east.
As Roman imperial governance contracted and the supply of Egyptian <color=#3366CC>papyrus</color> diminished, <color=#3366CC>parchment</color> became the
dominant writing material. Its vastly higher cost reinforced the clerical monopoly on literacy, which had declined with the
collapse of Roman municipal schools and civic structures that economically rewarded literate administrators. The
<color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> became the primary source of institutional continuity, legal memory, and administrative expertise for
the turbulent post-Roman kingdoms of Western Europe, which were contending with internecine warfare, barbarian
raids and invasions, and prolonged economic contraction. The Visigoths, Anglo-Saxons, Lombards, Frisians,
Thuringians, and <color=#3366CC>Bavarians</color> converted to Catholicism between 550 and 750 AD but the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad conquest of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Visigothic Kingdom in Iberia</color> — the most organized and legally sophisticated Germanic-Catholic kingdom of the era —
left the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of the Franks</color> ("Francia"), Kingdom of the Lombards (on the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color>) and <color=#3366CC>petty Anglo-Saxon</color>
<color=#3366CC>kingdoms</color> as the only significant Catholic realms. Among the other long-term effects of this era of Church cultural
dominance was the <color=#3366CC>dissolution of traditional European kinship networks</color>.

In 800, the <color=#3366CC>Frankish</color> king <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> was crowned Emperor by <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo III</color>, the <color=#3366CC>first western Roman emperor since</color>
<color=#3366CC>Romulus Augustus</color>. The conflict-filled relationship between the Church and monarchs became the most important
political fact of European history for the next 500 years. The stability of Charlemagne's reign, stimulated a brief revival
of cultural activity known as the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color>. The earliest recorded concept of Europe as a cultural sphere
(instead of simply a geographic term), comprising territories practicing Western Christianity was formed by <color=#3366CC>Alcuin of</color>
<color=#3366CC>York</color> in the late 8th century during the reign of Charlemagne.
The rediscovery of the <color=#3366CC>Justinian Code</color> in Western Europe early in the 10th century rekindled a passion for the discipline
of law, which crossed many of the re-forming boundaries between East and West. In the <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color> or <color=#3366CC>Frankish</color> west,
<color=#3366CC>Roman law</color> became the foundation on which all legal concepts and systems were based, influencing all Western legal
systems. The study of <color=#3366CC>canon law</color>, the legal system of the Catholic Church, fused with Roman law became the basis of
the refounding of Western legal scholarship.
In 1054 came the <color=#3366CC>Great Schism</color> that, following the Greek East and Latin West divide, separated Europe into religious
and cultural regions present to this day.
High Middle Ages and Renaissance
Medieval Christianity is credited with creating the first modern universities. The oldest university currently in continuous
operation in the world appeared in the 11th century in Italy (the <color=#3366CC>University of Bologna</color>) and two more were established
in the 12th century in France (the <color=#3366CC>University of Paris</color>) and England (the <color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>). With <color=#3366CC>Christian culture</color> as
the predominant force in Western civilization, the <color=#3366CC>Scholastic</color> movement of the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color> sought to connect
<color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color> with Greek thought. The economist <color=#3366CC>Joseph Schumpeter</color> asserted that medieval Scholastics "come nearer
than does any other group to having been the 'founders' of scientific economics." Though lost in the West, many
classical Greek texts were translated into Arabic and preserved in the <color=#3366CC>medieval Islamic world</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Greek classics</color> along
with <color=#3366CC>Arabic science</color>, philosophy and technology were transmitted to Western Europe and <color=#3366CC>translated into Latin</color>, sparking
the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance of the 12th century</color> and 13th century.
The <color=#3366CC>Sovereign Military Order of Malta</color>, which today has over 50,000 medical personnel, traces its origins to 1099 AD.
The Hospitallers of the Holy Spirit, which at its height operated hundreds of hospitals across Europe, was founded in
1180 AD. Medieval hospitals were established to cater to "social groups marginalized by poverty, sickness, and age,"
according to the historian and vastly improved upon the Roman valetudinaria and Greek healing temples. Christianity
also played a role in ending practices common among pagan societies, such as human sacrifice, slavery, infanticide
and polygamy. <color=#3366CC>Francisco de Vitoria</color>, a disciple of <color=#3366CC>Thomas Aquinas</color> and a Catholic thinker who studied the issue
regarding the human rights of colonized natives, is recognized by the United Nations as a father of international law,
and now also by historians of economics and democracy as a leading light for the West's democracy and rapid
economic development.
The 14th century <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, starting from Italy and then spreading throughout Europe, was associated with a
massive artistic, architectural and philosophical revival. Renaissance humanism advanced a <color=#3366CC>worldview</color> centered on
nature and the importance of humanity, emerging from the study of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> and influencing philosophy and
art for many years. In the following century, this process was enhanced by an exodus of Greek Christian priests and
scholars to Italian cities such as <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venice</color> after the fall of Constantinople.
From a single print shop in <color=#3366CC>Mainz</color>, Germany around 1440, <color=#3366CC>printing spread</color> to more than 270 cities in Europe and
produced more than 20 million volumes by the end of the 15th century. The technology ended the manuscript culture of
the Middle Ages, replacing it with a printing culture. At the same time, the number of universities exceeded 60.
Early modern era
By 1500 — two centuries before the Industrial Revolution and a century before the Scientific Revolution — Europe's
technology and advanced political and economic organization "[gave] it a decisive edge over all other civilizations on
earth." European navigators achieved the <color=#3366CC>first circumnavigation of Earth</color> at the beginning of the 16th century, including
the first crossing of the Pacific. During the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>, every continent except <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color> was visited and mapped
by Europeans.

Sparked by <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color>’s <color=#3366CC>Ninety-five Theses</color> (1517) and spread by the new <color=#3366CC>movable type</color> <color=#3366CC>printing press</color> in vernacular
languages (i.e. not Latin), the <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color> was a religious and political challenge to the <color=#3366CC>papacy</color> and the
authority of the Catholic Church hierarchy. As the movement branched into <color=#3366CC>Lutheranism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Calvinism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Anglicanism</color>, it
triggered the Catholic <color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color> and reshaped Europe’s political landscape. The upheaval of the
Reformation exploded into nearly <color=#3366CC>two centuries of religious wars</color> — the most devastating European conflicts until the
20th century — and resulted in millions of deaths, especially in Germany, where over a third of the population perished
from conflict, disease and famine.
<color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color>’s <color=#3366CC>early 17th-century telescopic observations</color> began the transformation of what had been a narrowly
technical revision of <color=#3366CC>classical astronomy</color> by <color=#3366CC>Nicolaus Copernicus</color> into an increasingly aggressive challenge to traditional
cosmology and the long-standing synthesis of Aristotelian physics and Christian theology. The upheaval of the
<color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> ended the medieval view of <color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color> as secondary to theology. As natural philosophy
grew in power and independence during the 17th century, European society began to dramatically change intellectual
attitude — from fides quaerens intellectum to a new mode of understanding that was decoupled from religion. The
"New Science" that emerged by the end of the century broke sharply with the natural philosophy that had preceded it,
departed from previous Greek conceptions and traditions, was more mechanistic in its worldview and more integrated
with mathematics, and was obsessed with the acquisition and interpretation of new evidence.
During the <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color> of the 18th century, cultural and intellectual forces in European society emphasized
reason, analysis, and individualism rather than traditional authority. It challenged the authority of deeply rooted social
institutions, such as the Catholic Church. Social reforms promoting toleration, science and <color=#3366CC>skepticism</color> became popular.
Philosophers of the Enlightenment included <color=#3366CC>John Locke</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baruch Spinoza</color>, <color=#3366CC>Voltaire</color> (1694–1778), <color=#3366CC>Jean-Jacques</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rousseau</color>, <color=#3366CC>David Hume</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Immanuel Kant</color>, who influenced society by publishing widely read works. Some rulers met
with intellectuals and applied reforms, such as allowing for toleration, or accepting multiple religions, in what became
known as <color=#3366CC>enlightened absolutism</color>. New ideas and beliefs spread around Europe, fostered by increased literacy made
possible by an emergence of non-religious publishing. Notable publications include <color=#3366CC>Encyclopédie</color> (1751–72) edited by
<color=#3366CC>Denis Diderot</color> and <color=#3366CC>Jean le Rond d'Alembert</color>, and the Dictionnaire philosophique (1764) and Letters on the English
(1733) by Voltaire.
Industrial Revolution
During the <color=#3366CC>Great Divergence</color>, the Western world overcame pre-modern growth constraints and emerged during the

19th century as the most powerful and wealthy world <color=#3366CC>civilization</color>, eclipsing <color=#3366CC>Qing China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mughal India</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa Japan</color>,
and the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>. European states colonized most of the planet; only thirteen present-day independent
countries escaped formal colonization by European powers. There are a many theories to explain the Great
Divergence, including lack of government intervention, high bridging social capital, geography, colonialism, and
customary traditions.
The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> was the transition to new manufacturing processes in the period from about 1760 to
sometime between 1820 and 1840. This included transitions from hand production methods to machines, new chemical
manufacturing and iron production processes, more efficient <color=#3366CC>water power</color>, increased use of <color=#3366CC>steam power</color>, and the
development of <color=#3366CC>machine tools</color>. These transitions began in Great Britain and spread to Western Europe and North
America within a few decades.
The Industrial Revolution marks a major turning point in history; almost every aspect of daily life was influenced. In
particular, average income and population began to exhibit unprecedented sustained growth. Some economists say
that the major impact of the Industrial Revolution was that the standard of living for the general population began to
increase consistently for the first time in history, although others have said that it did not begin to meaningfully improve
until the late 19th and 20th centuries while the Maddison Project argues that GDP per capita in Western Europe had
<color=#3366CC>diverged at least as early as 1400</color>. The precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution is still debated among
historians, as is the pace of economic and social changes. Economic historians agree that the onset of the Industrial
Revolution is the most important event in human history since the domestication of animals, plants and fire.
The First Industrial Revolution evolved into the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color> in the transition years between 1840 and
1870, when technological and economic progress continued with the adoption of steam transport (steam-powered
railways, boats, and ships), large-scale manufacture of machine tools and increased use of machinery in
steam-powered factories.
Post-Industrial era
Tendencies that have come to define modern Western societies include the concept of political pluralism, <color=#3366CC>individualism</color>,

prominent <color=#3366CC>subcultures</color> or <color=#3366CC>countercultures</color> (such as <color=#3366CC>New Age</color> movements) and increasing cultural <color=#3366CC>syncretism</color> resulting
from <color=#3366CC>globalization</color> and immigration. Western culture has been heavily influenced by the Renaissance, the Ages of
<color=#3366CC>Discovery</color> and Enlightenment and the <color=#3366CC>Industrial</color> and <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolutions</color>.
In the 20th century, Christianity declined in influence in many Western countries, mostly in the European Union where
most member states have experienced falling church attendance and membership. <color=#3366CC>Secularism</color>, the separation of
religion from politics and science increased. Christianity remains the dominant religion in the Western world, where
70% are Christians.
The West went through a series of great cultural and social changes between 1945 and 1980. Mass media including
film, radio, television and recorded music created a global culture that could ignore national frontiers. Literacy became
almost universal, encouraging the growth of books, magazines and newspapers. The influence of cinema and radio
remained, while televisions became near essentials in every home.
By the mid-20th century, Western culture was exported worldwide, and the development and growth of international
transport and telecommunication such as the transatlantic cable and radiotelephone played a decisive role in modern
globalization. The West has contributed to <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color>, democracy, industrialisation, and is the first
major civilization to seek to <color=#3366CC>abolish slavery</color> during the 19th century.
In the late 20th and early 21st centuries, the definition of the Western Culture solidified around institutional membership
in the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> and <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>, which serve as the primary geopolitical and security anchors of Western identity. For
<color=#3366CC>Central European</color> nations, the fall of the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color> in 1989 represented a "return to Europe," reclaiming a historical
identity rooted in Latin Christendom and Enlightenment values that had been suppressed during 42 years of <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>.
Historians like <color=#3366CC>Samuel Huntington</color> classify <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> as the "core state" of a distinct <color=#3366CC>Orthodox</color> civilization, separated from
the West by a centuries-old cultural "fault line". Some scholars trace Russia's autocratic tradition to the Mongol
conquest, which isolated <color=#3366CC>Muscovy</color> from Europe for centuries and ingrained a model of absolute, centralized power and
collective submission that never existed in the West.
Contemporary consensus defines Western culture not just by geography, but by a commitment to <color=#3366CC>liberal democratic</color>
<color=#3366CC>governance</color>, the <color=#3366CC>rule of law</color>, and collective security. Participation in these international organizations is widely viewed
as the definitive marker of a state's alignment with Western values, emphasizing a shared responsibility for stability and
human rights.
Arts and humanities
Music
Catholic monks developed the first forms of modern Western musical notation to standardize liturgy throughout the
worldwide Church, and an enormous body of religious music has been composed for it through the ages. This led
directly to the emergence and development of European classical music and its many derivatives. The <color=#3366CC>Baroque</color> style,
which encompassed music, art, and architecture, was particularly encouraged by the post-Reformation Catholic Church
as such forms offered a means of religious expression that was stirring and emotional, intended to stimulate religious
fervor.

The <color=#3366CC>symphony</color>, concerto, <color=#3366CC>sonata</color>, opera, and <color=#3366CC>oratorio</color> have their origins in Italy. Many <color=#3366CC>musical instruments</color> developed in
the West have come to see widespread use all over the world; among them are the guitar, violin, piano, <color=#3366CC>pipe organ</color>,
saxophone, trombone, clarinet, <color=#3366CC>accordion</color>, and the theremin. In turn, it has been claimed that some European
instruments have roots in earlier Eastern instruments that were adopted from the medieval Islamic world. The solo
piano, <color=#3366CC>symphony orchestra</color>, and the string quartet are also significant musical innovations of the West.
Painting and photography
<color=#3366CC>Jan van Eyck</color>, among other renaissance painters, made great advances in <color=#3366CC>oil painting</color>, and <color=#3366CC>perspective</color> drawings and
paintings had their earliest practitioners in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>. In art, the Celtic knot is a very distinctive Western repeated motif.
Depictions of the nude human male and female in photography, painting, and sculpture are frequently considered to
have special artistic merit. Realistic <color=#3366CC>portraiture</color> is especially valued.
Dance and performing arts
The ballet is a distinctively Western form of performance dance. The <color=#3366CC>ballroom dance</color> is an important Western variety of
dance for the elite. The <color=#3366CC>polka</color>, the <color=#3366CC>square dance</color>, the <color=#3366CC>flamenco</color>,(which however has been long been framed in
<color=#3366CC>Orientalist</color> frameworks) and the Irish step dance are very well known Western forms of <color=#3366CC>folk dance</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Greek</color> and <color=#3366CC>Roman theatre</color> are considered the antecedents of modern theatre, and forms such as <color=#3366CC>medieval theatre</color>,
Passion Plays, morality plays, and <color=#3366CC>commedia dell'arte</color> are considered highly influential. Elizabethan theatre, with
playwrights including <color=#3366CC>William Shakespeare</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christopher Marlowe</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ben Jonson</color>, is considered one of the most
formative and important eras for modern drama.
The soap opera, a popular culture dramatic form, originated in the United States first on radio in the 1930s, then a
couple of decades later on television. The music video was also developed in the West in the middle of the 20th
century. Musical theatre was developed in the West in the 19th and 20th Centuries, from <color=#3366CC>music hall</color>, comic opera, and
<color=#3366CC>Vaudeville</color>; with significant contributions from the Jewish diaspora, African-Americans, and other marginalized peoples.
Literature
Western literature encompasses the literary traditions of Europe, as well as North America, Oceania and Latin America.
While epic literary works in verse such as the <color=#3366CC>Mahabharata</color> and Homer's <color=#3366CC>Iliad</color> are ancient and occurred worldwide, the
prose novel as a distinct form of storytelling, with developed, consistent human characters and, typically, some
connected overall plot (although both of these characteristics have sometimes been modified and played with in later
times), was popularized by the West in the 17th and 18th centuries. Of course, extended prose fiction had existed
much earlier; both novels of adventure and romance in the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic</color> world and in <color=#3366CC>Heian</color> Japan. Both Petronius'
Satyricon (c. 60 CE) and the <color=#3366CC>Tale of Genji</color> by <color=#3366CC>Murasaki Shikibu</color> (c. 1000 CE) have been cited as the world's first major
novel but they had a very limited long-term impact on literary writing beyond their own day until much more recent
times.
<color=#3366CC>Tragedy</color>, from its ritually and mythologically inspired Greek origins to modern forms where struggle and downfall are
often rooted in psychological or social, rather than mythical, motives, is also widely considered a specifically European
creation and can be seen as a forerunner of some aspects of both the novel and of classical opera.
Architecture
Important Western architectural motifs include the Doric, Corinthian, and Ionic orders of <color=#3366CC>Greek architecture</color>, and the

<color=#3366CC>Romanesque</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baroque</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Victorian</color> styles, which are still widely recognized and used in
contemporary Western architecture. Much of Western architecture emphasizes repetition of simple motifs, straight lines
and expansive, undecorated planes. A modern ubiquitous architectural form that emphasizes this characteristic is the
<color=#3366CC>skyscraper</color>, their modern equivalent first developed in New York and Chicago. The predecessor of the skyscraper can
be found in the medieval towers erected in Bologna.
Cuisine
Western foodways were, until recently, considered to have their roots in the cuisines of Classical Rome and Greece,
but the influence of Arab and <color=#3366CC>Near Eastern cuisine</color> on the West has become a topic of research in recent decades. The
<color=#3366CC>Crusaders</color>, known mostly for fighting over holy land, settled in the Levant and acclimated to the local culture and
cuisine. Fulcher of Chartres said "For we who were occidentals have now become orientals." These cultural
experiences, carried back to France by notables like <color=#3366CC>Eleanor of Aquitaine</color> influenced Western European foodways.
Many Oriental ingredients were relatively new to the Western lands. Sugar, almonds, pistachios, rosewater, and dried
citrus fruits were all novelties to the Crusaders who encountered them in Saracen lands. Pepper, ginger and cinnamon
were the most widely used spices of the European courts and noble households. By the end of the Middle Ages,
<color=#3366CC>cloves</color>, <color=#3366CC>nutmeg</color>, mastic, <color=#3366CC>galingale</color>, and other imported spices had become part of the Western cuisine.
Saracen influence can be seen in medieval cookbooks. Some recipes retain their Arabic names in Italian translations of
the Liber de Coquina. Known as bruet Sarassinois in the cuisine of North France, the concept of sweet and sour sauce
is attested to in Greek tradition when Anthimus finishes his stew with vinegar and honey. Saracens combined sweet
ingredients like date-juice and honey with pomegranate, lemons and citrus juices, or other sour ingredients. The
technique of browning pieces of meat and simmering in liquid with vegetables is used in many recipes from the
Baghdad cookery book. The same technique appears in the late-13th century Viandier. Fried pieces of beef simmered
in wine with sugar and cloves was called bruet of Sarcynesse in English.
Scientific and technological inventions and discoveries
Historians of science generally note that from the early modern period onward, scientific research in Europe became
increasingly institutionalized, contributing to the development of modern scientific methods and technologies. The
<color=#3366CC>scientific method</color> as "a method or procedure that has characterized natural science since the 17th century, consisting in
systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses"
was significantly shaped by the work of the 17th-century Italian scientist <color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color>, with roots in the work of
medieval scholars such as the 11th-century Iraqi physicist <color=#3366CC>Ibn al-Haytham</color> and the 13th-century English friar <color=#3366CC>Roger</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bacon</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> is credited with the invention of the <color=#3366CC>steam engine</color> and adapting its use into factories, and for the

generation of <color=#3366CC>electric power</color>. The electrical <color=#3366CC>motor</color>, <color=#3366CC>dynamo</color>, <color=#3366CC>transformer</color>, <color=#3366CC>electric light</color>, and most of the familiar electrical
appliances, were developed primarily in the United States and United Kingdom. The <color=#3366CC>Otto</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Diesel</color> <color=#3366CC>internal</color>
<color=#3366CC>combustion engines</color> are products whose genesis and early development were in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. <color=#3366CC>Nuclear power</color> stations are
derived from the first <color=#3366CC>atomic pile</color> constructed in Chicago in 1942.
Several communication devices and systems such as the <color=#3366CC>telegraph</color> and telephone were developed or commercialized
in Europe and North America during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
Ubiquitous materials were primarily discovered and developed in Europe and the United States. Iron and steel ships
first appeared in the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, and bridges and skyscrapers first appeared in the United States. <color=#3366CC>Nitrogen fixation</color>
and <color=#3366CC>petrochemicals</color> were invented in <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>transistor</color>, <color=#3366CC>integrated circuit</color>, memory chip, first <color=#3366CC>programming language</color>, computer, and the first powered airplane
was created in the United States.

In mathematics, many modern formal frameworks—such as <color=#3366CC>calculus</color>, statistics, <color=#3366CC>logic</color>, <color=#3366CC>vectors</color>, <color=#3366CC>tensors</color>, <color=#3366CC>complex</color>

<color=#3366CC>analysis</color>, <color=#3366CC>group theory</color>, <color=#3366CC>abstract algebra</color>, and <color=#3366CC>topology</color>—were developed and systematized primarily in Europe during
the early modern and modern periods, building on earlier contributions from ancient Greek, Indian, Islamic, and other
mathematical traditions. In biology, several foundational theories of modern biology—including <color=#3366CC>evolution</color>, <color=#3366CC>genetics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>chromosomes</color>, the structure of <color=#3366CC>DNA</color>, and the methods of <color=#3366CC>molecular biology</color>—were developed primarily in Europe and
North America during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, drawing on earlier global traditions in natural history and

medicine. In physics, major modern theories such as <color=#3366CC>mechanics</color>, <color=#3366CC>thermodynamics</color>, <color=#3366CC>statistical mechanics</color>, <color=#3366CC>relativity</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>quantum mechanics</color> were formulated chiefly within European scientific institutions, while incorporating insights from
earlier scientific traditions worldwide. Key discoveries made by European scientists in <color=#3366CC>electromagnetism</color> include
<color=#3366CC>Coulomb's law</color> (1785), the first <color=#3366CC>battery</color> (1800), the unity of electricity and magnetism (1820), <color=#3366CC>Biot–Savart law</color> (1820),
<color=#3366CC>Ohm's law</color> (1827), and <color=#3366CC>Maxwell's equations</color> (1871).
The most widely adopted system of measurement, the <color=#3366CC>International System of Units</color>, derived from the <color=#3366CC>metric system</color>,
was first developed in France and evolved through contributions from various Western countries.
In business, economics, and finance, <color=#3366CC>double-entry bookkeeping</color> was first used in <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>. Credit cards and the charge
card were first used in the United States.
Western countries played a major role in explorations of the globe and <color=#3366CC>outer space</color>. The first expedition to
<color=#3366CC>circumnavigate the Earth</color> (1522) was led by <color=#3366CC>Ferdinand Magellan</color>, as well as the first journey to the South Pole (1911)
by <color=#3366CC>Roald Amundsen</color>, and the first Moon landing (1969) by <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>. The landing of robots on Mars (2004 and 2012) and

on an asteroid (2001), the <color=#3366CC>Voyager 2</color> explorations of the outer planets (<color=#3366CC>Uranus</color> in 1986 and <color=#3366CC>Neptune</color> in 1989), <color=#3366CC>Voyager</color>
<color=#3366CC>1</color>s passage into interstellar space (2013), and <color=#3366CC>New Horizons</color> flyby of <color=#3366CC>Pluto</color> (2015) were significant recent achievements
of the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>.
Media
The roots of modern-day Western mass media can be traced back to the late 15th century, when <color=#3366CC>printing presses</color>
began to operate throughout wealthy European cities. The emergence of news media in the 17th century has to be
seen in close connection with the spread of the printing press, from which the publishing <color=#3366CC>press</color> derives its name.
In the 16th century, a decrease in the preeminence of <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> in its literary use, along with the impact of economic
change, the discoveries arising from trade and travel, navigation to the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, science and arts and the
development of increasingly rapid communications through print led to a rising corpus of vernacular media content in
European society.
After the launch of the satellite <color=#3366CC>Sputnik 1</color> by the Soviet Union in 1957, satellite transmission technology was
dramatically realized, with the United States launching Telstar in 1962 linking live media broadcasts from the UK to the
US. The first digital broadcast satellite (DBS) system began transmitting in US in 1975.
Beginning in the 1990s, the Internet has contributed to a tremendous increase in the accessibility of Western media
content. Departing from media offered in bundled content packages (magazines, CDs, <color=#3366CC>television and radio slots</color>), the
Internet has primarily offered unbundled content items (articles, audio and video files).
Religion
The native religions of Europe were <color=#3366CC>polytheistic</color> but not homogeneous – however, they were similar insofar as they
were predominantly <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color> in origin. <color=#3366CC>Roman religion</color> was similar to but not the same as <color=#3366CC>Hellenic religion</color> –
likewise for <color=#3366CC>indigenous Germanic polytheism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Celtic polytheism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Slavic polytheism</color>. Before this time many
Europeans from the north, especially Scandinavians, remained polytheistic, though southern Europe was
predominantly Christian from the 5th century onwards.
Western culture at a fundamental level is influenced by the Judeo-Christian and Greco-Roman traditions. These
cultures had a number of similarities, such as a common emphasis on the individual, but they also embody
fundamentally conflicting worldviews. For example, in Judaism and Christianity, God is the ultimate authority, while
Greco-Roman tradition considers the ultimate authority to be <color=#3366CC>reason</color>. Christian attempts to reconcile these frameworks
were responsible for the preservation of <color=#3366CC>Greek philosophy</color>. Historically, Europe has been the center and cradle of
Christian civilization.
According to a survey by Pew Research Center from 2011, Christianity remains the dominant religion in the Western
world where 70–84% are Christians, According to this survey, 76% of Europeans described themselves as Christians,
and about 86% of the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>' population identified themselves as Christians, (90% in Latin America and 77% in
North America). 73% in Oceania self-identify as Christian, and 76% in South Africa are Christian.
Eurobarometer polls about religiosity in the European Union in 2012 found that Christianity was the largest religion in
the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, accounting for 72% of the population. <color=#3366CC>Catholics</color> are the largest <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> group, accounting for
48%, while <color=#3366CC>Protestants</color> make up 12%, <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color> make up 8% and other Christians make up 4% of the
population respectively. In addition, <color=#3366CC>non-believers/agnostics</color> account for 16%, <color=#3366CC>atheists</color> account for 7%, and <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>
account for 2% of the population respectively. According to Scholars, in 2017, Europe's population was 77.8% Christian
(up from 74.9% 1970), these changes were largely ascribed to the <color=#3366CC>collapse of Communism</color> and switching to
Christianity in the former Soviet Union and <color=#3366CC>Eastern Bloc</color> countries.
At the same time, there has been an increase in the share of agnostic or <color=#3366CC>atheist</color> residents in Europe that accounted for
18% of the European population in 2012. In particular, over half of the population of the <color=#3366CC>Czech Republic</color> (79%) was
agnostic, atheist or irreligious, compared to the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> (52%), <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> (25–33%), <color=#3366CC>France</color> (30–35%) and the
<color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color> (39–44%).
As in other areas, the Jewish diaspora and Judaism exist in the Western world.
There are also small but increasing numbers of people across the Western world who seek to revive the indigenous
religions of their European ancestors; such <color=#3366CC>groups</color> include <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, Roman, Hellenic, Celtic, Slavic, and polytheistic
reconstructionist movements. Likewise, <color=#3366CC>Wicca</color>, New Age spirituality and other <color=#3366CC>neo-pagan</color> belief systems enjoy notable
minority support in Western states.
Sport
Since <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>, sport has been an important facet of Western cultural expression.
A wide range of sports was already established by the time of <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greece</color> and the military culture and the
development of sports in Greece influenced one another considerably. Sports became such a prominent part of their
culture that the Greeks created the <color=#3366CC>Olympic Games</color>, which in ancient times were held every four years in a small village
in the <color=#3366CC>Peloponnesus</color> called <color=#3366CC>Olympia</color>. Baron <color=#3366CC>Pierre de Coubertin</color>, a Frenchman, instigated the modern revival of the
Olympic movement. The first modern Olympic games were held at Athens in 1896.
The Romans built immense structures such as the amphitheatres to house their festivals of sport. The Romans
exhibited a passion for <color=#3366CC>blood sports</color>, such as the infamous <color=#3366CC>Gladiatorial</color> battles that pitted contestants against one
another in a fight to the death. The Olympic Games revived many of the sports of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>—such as

<color=#3366CC>Greco-Roman wrestling</color>, <color=#3366CC>discus</color> and <color=#3366CC>javelin</color>. The sport of <color=#3366CC>bullfighting</color> is a traditional spectacle of Spain, Portugal,
southern France, and some Latin American countries. It traces its roots to prehistoric bull worship and <color=#3366CC>sacrifice</color> and is
often linked to Rome, where many human-versus-animal events were held. Bullfighting spread from Spain to its
American colonies, and in the 19th century to France, where it developed into a distinctive form in its own right.
<color=#3366CC>Jousting</color> and hunting were popular sports in the European Middle Ages, and the aristocratic classes developed
passions for leisure activities. A great number of popular global sports were first developed or codified in Europe. The
modern game of <color=#3366CC>golf</color> originated in Scotland, where the first written record of golf is <color=#3366CC>James II</color>'s banning of the game in
1457, as an unwelcome distraction to learning <color=#3366CC>archery</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> that began in Great Britain in the 18th century brought increased leisure time, leading to more
opportunities for citizens to participate in athletic activities and also follow spectator sports. These trends continued with
the advent of mass media and global communication. The bat and ball sport of <color=#3366CC>cricket</color> was first played in England
during the 16th century and was exported around the globe via the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color>. A number of popular modern sports
were devised or codified in the United Kingdom during the 19th century and obtained global prominence; these include
<color=#3366CC>ping pong</color>, modern <color=#3366CC>tennis</color>, association football, <color=#3366CC>netball</color> and <color=#3366CC>rugby</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Football</color> (or soccer) remains hugely popular in Europe, but has grown from its origins to be known as the world game.
Similarly, sports such as cricket, rugby, and netball were exported around the world, particularly among countries in the
<color=#3366CC>Commonwealth of Nations</color>, thus India and Australia are among the strongest cricketing states, while victory in the
<color=#3366CC>Rugby World Cup</color> has been shared among New Zealand, Australia, England, and South Africa.
<color=#3366CC>Australian Rules Football</color>, an Australian variation of football with similarities to <color=#3366CC>Gaelic football</color> and <color=#3366CC>rugby</color>, evolved in the
British colony of Victoria in the mid-19th century. The United States also developed unique variations of English sports.
English migrants took antecedents of <color=#3366CC>baseball</color> to America during the colonial period. The history of <color=#3366CC>American football</color>
can be traced to early versions of rugby football and association football. Many games are known as "football" were
being played at colleges and universities in the United States in the first half of the 19th century. American football
resulted from several major divergences from rugby, most notably the rule changes instituted by <color=#3366CC>Walter Camp</color>, the
"Father of American football". <color=#3366CC>Basketball</color> was invented in 1891 by <color=#3366CC>James Naismith</color>, a Canadian physical education
instructor working in Springfield, Massachusetts, in the United States. <color=#3366CC>Volleyball</color> was created in Holyoke,
Massachusetts, a city directly north of Springfield, in 1895.
Themes and traditions
Western culture has developed many themes and traditions, the most significant of which are:
• Greco-Roman classic letters, arts, architecture, philosophical and cultural tradition, which include the influence of

preeminent authors and philosophers such as <color=#3366CC>Socrates</color>, <color=#3366CC>Plato</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Homer</color>, <color=#3366CC>Virgil</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Cicero</color>, as well as a
long <color=#3366CC>mythologic tradition</color>.
• Christian ethical, philosophical, and <color=#3366CC>mythological</color> tradition, stemming largely from the <color=#3366CC>Christian Bible</color>, particularly
the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color> Gospels.
• Monasteries, schools, libraries, books, book making, universities, teaching, education, and lecture halls.
• A tradition of the importance of <color=#3366CC>the rule of law</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Secular humanism</color>, <color=#3366CC>rationalism</color> and Enlightenment thought. This set the basis for a new critical attitude and open
questioning of religion, favouring <color=#3366CC>freethinking</color> and questioning of the church as an authority, which resulted in
open-minded and reformist ideals inside, such as <color=#3366CC>liberation theology</color>, which partly adopted these currents, and
secular and political tendencies such as <color=#3366CC>separation of church and state</color> (sometimes termed laicism), agnosticism
and <color=#3366CC>atheism</color>.
• Generalized usage of some form of the <color=#3366CC>Latin alphabet</color>, used by the majority of Europe, <color=#3366CC>Greek alphabet</color>, used in
Greece. Other variants of the Latin or Greek alphabets are found in the Gothic and Coptic alphabets, which
historically superseded older scripts, such as <color=#3366CC>runes</color>, and the Egyptian Demotic and <color=#3366CC>Hieroglyphic</color> systems.

• <color=#3366CC>Natural law</color>, human rights, constitutionalism, <color=#3366CC>parliamentarism</color> (or <color=#3366CC>presidentialism</color>) and formal <color=#3366CC>liberal democracy</color> in
recent times—prior to the 19th century, most Western governments were still monarchies.
• A large influence, in <color=#3366CC>modern times</color>, of many of the ideals and values developed and inherited from <color=#3366CC>Romanticism</color>.
• An emphasis on, and use of, science as a means of understanding the natural world and humanity's place in it.
• More pronounced use and application of innovation and scientific developments, as well as a more rational
approach to scientific progress (what has been known as the <color=#3366CC>scientific method</color>).
Roman Forum
The Roman Forum (Italian: Foro Romano), also known by its <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> name Forum Romanum, is a rectangular forum
(<color=#3366CC>plaza</color>) surrounded by the ruins of several important ancient government buildings at the centre of the city of <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>.
Citizens of the ancient city referred to this space, originally a marketplace, as the Forum Magnum, or simply the Forum.
For centuries, the Forum was the centre of day-to-day life in Rome: the site of triumphal processions and elections; the
venue for public speeches, criminal trials and <color=#3366CC>gladiatorial matches</color>; and the nucleus of commercial and legal affairs.
Here statues and monuments commemorated the city's leaders. The heart of <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>, it has been called the
most celebrated meeting place in the world, and in all history. Located in the small valley between the Palatine and
<color=#3366CC>Capitoline Hills</color>, the Forum today is a sprawling ruin of architectural fragments and intermittent archaeological
excavations attracting 4.5 million or more sightseers yearly.
Many of the oldest and most important structures of the ancient city were located on or near the Forum. The <color=#3366CC>Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom</color>'s earliest shrines and temples were located on the southeastern edge. These included the ancient former
royal residence, the Regia (8th century BC), and the Temple of Vesta (7th century BC), as well as the surrounding
complex of the Vestal Virgins, all of which were rebuilt after the rise of <color=#3366CC>imperial Rome</color>.
Other archaic shrines to the northwest, such as the Umbilicus Urbis and the Vulcanal (Shrine of Vulcan), developed
into the <color=#3366CC>Republic</color>'s formal Comitium (assembly area). This was where the <color=#3366CC>Senate</color>—as well as <color=#3366CC>Republican government</color>
itself—began. The Senate House, government offices, tribunals, temples, memorials and statues gradually cluttered
the area.
Over time, the archaic Comitium was replaced by the larger adjacent Forum, and the focus of judicial activity moved to
the new Basilica Aemilia (179 BC), formally Basilica Fulvia. Some 130 years later, <color=#3366CC>Julius Caesar</color> built the Basilica Julia,
along with the new Curia Julia, refocusing both the judicial offices and the Senate itself. This new Forum, in what
proved to be its final form, then served as a revitalized city square where the people of Rome could gather for
commercial, political, <color=#3366CC>judicial</color> and <color=#3366CC>religious</color> pursuits in ever greater numbers.
Eventually, much economic and judicial business would transfer away from the Forum Romanum to the larger and
more extravagant structures (Trajan's Forum and the Basilica Ulpia) to the north. The reign of <color=#3366CC>Constantine the Great</color>
saw the construction of the last major expansion of the Forum complex—the Basilica of Maxentius (312 AD). This
returned the political centre to the Forum until the fall of the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color> almost two centuries later.
Description
Unlike the later imperial fora in Rome—which were self-consciously modelled on the ancient Greek plateia public plaza
or <color=#3366CC>town square</color>—the Roman Forum developed gradually, organically, and piecemeal over many centuries. This is the
case despite attempts, with some success, to impose some order there, by <color=#3366CC>Sulla</color>, <color=#3366CC>Julius Caesar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Augustus</color> and others.
By the Imperial period, the large public buildings that crowded around the central square had reduced the open area to
a rectangle of about 130 by 50 meters.
Its long dimension was oriented northwest to southeast and extended from the foot of the <color=#3366CC>Capitoline Hill</color> to that of the
Velian Hill. The Forum's <color=#3366CC>basilicas</color> during the Imperial period—the Basilica Aemilia on the north and the Basilica Julia on
the south—defined its long sides and its final form. The Forum proper included this square, the buildings facing it and,
sometimes, an additional area (the Forum Adjectum) extending southeast as far as the Arch of Titus.
Originally, the site of the Forum had been a <color=#3366CC>marshy</color> lake where waters from the surrounding hills drained. This was
drained by the Tarquins with the Cloaca Maxima. Because of its location, sediments from both the flooding of the <color=#3366CC>Tiber</color>
and the erosion of the surrounding hills have been raising the level of the Forum floor for centuries. Excavated
sequences of remains of paving show that sediment eroded from the surrounding hills was already raising the level in
early <color=#3366CC>Republican</color> times.
As the ground around buildings rose, residents simply paved over the debris that was too much to remove. Its final
travertine paving, still visible, dates from the reign of <color=#3366CC>Augustus</color>. Excavations in the 19th century revealed one layer on
top of another. The deepest level excavated was 3.60 meters <color=#3366CC>above sea level</color>. Archaeological finds show human
activity at that level with the discovery of carbonized wood.
An important function of the Forum, during both Republican and Imperial times, was to serve as the culminating venue
for the celebratory military processions known as Triumphs. Victorious generals entered the city by the western
Triumphal Gate (Porta Triumphalis) and circumnavigated the Palatine Hill (counterclockwise) before proceeding from
the Velian Hill down the Via Sacra and into the Forum.
From here, they would mount the Capitoline Rise (Clivus Capitolinus) up to the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on
the summit of the Capitol. Lavish public banquets ensued back down on the Forum. (In addition to the Via Sacra, the
Forum was accessed by several storied roads and streets, including the Vicus Jugarius, Vicus Tuscus, Argiletum, and
Via Nova.)
History
Pre-Roman Period
Pottery deposits discovered in the Forum, Palatine and Capitoline demonstrated that humans occupied these areas in
the Final Bronze Age (1200–975 BC). In the early Iron Age an area of the future Forum, close to the site of Temple of
Antoninus and Faustina, was used as a cemetery (10th century BC), possibly by the communities based on the
Palatine and Capitoline hills. Most of the burials were cremations of the same type which is also found in the other sites
in Latium. The urn containing the ashes of the deceased was placed inside a large earthenware jar, along with grave
goods, and then buried in a cavity cut into the ground and covered with a capstone. There were also a small number of
inhumation burials. On current evidence, it is likely that burials in the Forum ceased in the late 9th century BC and that
the Esquiline Necropolis replaced them.
The first archaeological finds on the sites of the key public buildings point to a transformation of the Forum from a
cemetery to a public site in the 8th century BC. Part of the Forum was paved over. The earliest finds in the sites of the
Comitium and Vulcanal were votive offerings. They indicate that the area was dedicated to a celebration of religious
cults.
Roman Kingdom
Roman historical tradition
According to Roman historical tradition, the Forum's beginnings are connected with the alliance between <color=#3366CC>Romulus</color>, the
first king of Rome controlling the Palatine Hill, and his rival, Titus Tatius, who occupied the <color=#3366CC>Capitoline Hill</color>. An alliance
formed after combat had been halted by the prayers and cries of the Sabine women. Because the valley lay between
the two settlements, it was the designated place for the two peoples to meet. Since the early Forum area included
pools of stagnant water, the most easily accessible area was the northern part of the valley which was designated as
the Comitium. It was here at the Vulcanal that, according to the story, the two parties laid down their weapons and
formed an alliance.
The Forum was outside the walls of the original Sabine fortress, which was entered through the Porta Saturni. These
walls were mostly destroyed when the two hills were joined. The original Forum functioned as an open-air market
abutting on the Comitium, but eventually outgrew its day-to-day shopping and marketplace role. As political speeches,
civil trials, and other public affairs began to take up more and more space in the Forum, additional fora throughout the
city began to emerge to expand on specific needs of the growing population. Fora for cattle, pork, vegetables and wine
specialised in their niche products and the associated deities.
Rome's second king, Numa Pompilius (r. 715–673 BC), is said to have begun the cult of Vesta, building its house and
temple as well as the Regia as the city's first royal palace. Later Tullus Hostilius (r. 673–642 BC) enclosed the
Comitium around the old Etruscan temple where the <color=#3366CC>Senate</color> would meet at the site of the Sabine conflict. He is said to
have converted that temple into the Curia Hostilia close to where the Senate originally met in an old Etruscan hut. In
600 BC Tarquinius Priscus had the area paved for the first time.
Archaeological evidence
Originally a low-lying, grassy <color=#3366CC>wetland</color>, the Forum was drained in the 7th century BC with the building of the first
structures of Cloaca Maxima, a large covered sewer system that emptied into the <color=#3366CC>Tiber</color>, as more people began to settle
between the two hills. Archaeological evidence shows that by the end of the 7th century BC, the ground level of the
Forum was raised significantly in some places to overcome the problems of poor drainage and provide a foundation for
a pebble-paved area. In the middle of the 7th century BC thatch-and-timber huts were demolished on the route of the
Via Sacra and rectangular stone buildings began to replace them.
The earliest structures in the Forum were discovered in two separate locations: the site of the Comitium and the group
of sanctuaries of Regia (House of the kings), House of the Vestals and Domus Publica. Around 650–630 BC the area
of the Comitium was excavated into a deep triangular depression. The area was paved with a beaten earth pavement
and later replaced with a more substantial gravel one. Nearby was located an archaic sanctuary dedicated to <color=#3366CC>Vulcan</color>
known as Vulcanal (also Volcanal): a small rectangular pit and elliptical basin carved out of an outcrop of <color=#3366CC>tuff</color>. It has
been suggested that the earliest ancient materials collected in the area of the Vulcanal are from the second half of the
8th century BC. It appears that the Romans were aware of the sites’ archaic origins: the foundation of the Comitium
and Vulcanal were attributed to Romulus himself while the first Curia (senate house), which was located nearby, to
Tullus Hostilius.
At the western end of the Forum, excavations near the House of the Vestals and the sanctuary of Vesta have revealed
an important group of 7th-century-BC buildings. The archaeologists have identified them as the early phases of the
Regia (House of the kings), House of the Vestals, and Domus Publica (official residence of the pontifex maximus).
There seems to have been something of a surge in development of the Forum in the last quarter of the 7th century BC,
as many of the changes date from 625 to 600 BC. Archaeologically, there is substantial evidence for development of
the Forum in the 6th century BC: parts of the paving have been found and a large number of fragments of terracotta
decorations from this area suggests that structures around the Forum were becoming more elaborate and highly
decorated.
Roman Republic
During the Republican period, the Comitium continued to be the central location for all judicial and political life in the
city. However, to create a larger gathering place, the Senate began expanding the open area between the Comitium
and the Temple of Vesta by purchasing existing private homes and removing them for public use. Building projects of
several consuls repaved and built onto both the Comitium and the adjacent central plaza that was becoming the Forum.
The 5th century BC witnessed the earliest Forum temples with known dates of construction: the Temple of Saturn (497
BC) and the Temple of Castor and Pollux (484 BC). The Temple of Concord was added in the following century,
possibly by the soldier and statesman Marcus Furius Camillus. A long-held tradition of speaking from the elevated
speakers' Rostra—originally facing north towards the Senate House to the assembled politicians and elites—put the
orator's back to the people assembled in the Forum. A tribune known as Caius Licinius (consul in 361 BC) is said to
have been the first to turn away from the elite towards the Forum, an act symbolically repeated two centuries later by
<color=#3366CC>Gaius Gracchus</color>.
This began the tradition of locus popularis, in which even young nobles were expected to speak to the people from the
Rostra. Gracchus was thus credited with (or accused of) disturbing the mos maiorum ("custom of the
fathers/ancestors") in ancient Rome. When Censor in 318 BC, Gaius Maenius provided buildings in the Forum
neighborhood with balconies, which were called after him maeniana, so that the spectators might better view the
games put on within the temporary wooden arenas set up there.
The Tribune benches were placed on the Forum Romanum, as well. First, they stood next to the senate house; during
the late Roman Republic, they were placed in front of the Basilica Porcia.
The earliest <color=#3366CC>basilicas</color> (large, aisled halls) were introduced to the Forum in 184 BC by <color=#3366CC>Marcus Porcius Cato</color>, who thus
began the process of "monumentalizing" the site. The Basilica Fulvia was dedicated on the north side of the Forum
square in 179 BC. (It was rebuilt and renamed several times, as Basilica Fulvia et Aemilia, Basilica Paulli, Basilica
